title: Glossary: The Language of Listing Systems
basis: Reconstructed on 2026-11-12 from the published page (posts/glossary/index.md) and its former spec.md (accepted 2026-10-21), which it replaces; one spec paragraph per prose unit of the page, in the page's order. Intent outcome, AC-1 to AC-3 and role are copied unchanged from the post's entry in journal-spec.json. The journal spec gives this post no thesis, so the thesis and its four supporting claims are written here from the entry's question, the Reference part's claim R-2 and the published callouts. The page is a reference page: its content is about 405 definition rows in eleven tables and an alphabetical index, which are not prose units; the spec's units are the prose paragraphs, each section's lead paragraph with its table as evidence, and the index list with its lead-in. The three callouts (IN THIS SECTION, KEY POINTS, FAILURE PATTERNS) stand before the first paragraph as the house format. Changes to the published page made to meet the contract: a new opening paragraph (p01) before the published 'How to Use This Glossary' heading carries the bridge from the toolkit, the hook, the thesis and the announcement of that section; each part section's lead sentence was reworded to state how it follows the previous section; a lead-in sentence was added before the alphabetical index; and a synthesis paragraph (p15) was added after the index, before the published closing pointer. No definition, owning-chapter link, figure or name was changed; the GMV row was moved from Part I to Part VI, whose chapter owns it.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given a pair of terms that are often confused, the reader finds both on the page, states the difference in their own words and names the owning chapter.
acceptance_criteria.probe: Using only this page: what is the difference between a contact, a conversation and a lead, and between the publication state and the enforcement overlay of a listing? Which chapter owns each pair?
acceptance_criteria.expected: A contact is any action by which a buyer reaches a seller about a listing (a message, form, call, callback, booking or application); a conversation is the platform-held thread of messages about one listing; a lead is a record, created by a defined rule, that a specific buyer expressed interest in a professional's listing, delivered to that professional and tracked to an outcome (all messaging-and-leads). The publication state is owned by the listing (draft, active, sold, expired and so on); the enforcement overlay is owned by trust and safety (none, held, restricted, blocked, restored); visibility and contactability are derived from both (listing-aggregate).

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader of the opening alone can say how the page is organized and how to use it.
acceptance_criteria.probe: After reading only the callouts and the paragraphs before the first heading: how is this page organized, and how should you use it?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Sections grouped by part (evidence labels and failure patterns, Parts I to VIII, Veldmark names) with an alphabetical index at the end; look a term up, read its neighbors for the contrasts, follow the link to the owning chapter; one term, one meaning, one owning chapter, and a disagreement with a chapter is a defect; regulatory and company terms are dated as of 2026 and must be checked before use.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reverse outline of the page, written without the spec, lists the same controlling ideas in the same order as the post spec's sections and paragraphs.
Given an abbreviation, the reader uses the alphabetical index to reach its row and names what it stands for, the section that defines it and the chapter that owns it.
acceptance_criteria.probe: Using only this page: you meet the abbreviation 'ATO' in a design review. How do you find it on this page, what does it stand for, in which section is it defined, and which chapter or chapters own it?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Through the alphabetical index (under A), which links ATO to the Part V — Trust section; ATO is account takeover (credentials phished or stuffed so that an aged, reputable account posts scam listings or redirects payouts); the owning chapters are fraud-prevention and identity-and-verification.

thesis.question: What does each of the book's terms mean, which terms is it most often confused with, and which chapter owns it?
thesis.claim: Each of the book's terms has exactly one meaning, the one its owning chapter teaches, and the terms most often confused (listing and underlying entity, publication state and enforcement overlay, full snapshot and delta feed, contact, conversation and lead, entitlement and effect, system of record and read model) differ in what they count and who owns them, so a reader should look a term up beside its neighbors, follow it to its owning chapter and treat any disagreement between a chapter and this page as a defect to fix.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that a glossary is an alphabetical word list for occasional reference, in which near-synonyms such as contact and lead can be used loosely and each team may keep its own meaning of a term as long as it documents it locally.
thesis.so_what: A reader uses one meaning per term across metrics, contracts, templates and teams, settles a disputed term by its owning chapter's worked example, and checks a regulatory or company term against its current source before it goes into a contract, a policy or a design decision.
thesis.how_why: When 'contact' means a message in one warehouse, a lead in another and a phone reveal in a third, the group steers on numbers that cannot be compared (Vanity Liquidity); one concept under several names, or one name for several concepts, leaves filters, feeds, models and teams disagreeing about what a listing is (The Attribute Junkyard). Grouping the terms by part puts the confusable ones in one row or adjacent rows, the owning-chapter link sends the reader to the chapter whose worked example settles the meaning, and dating regulatory and company terms as of 2026 tells the reader when to look again.

supporting_claims.claim: The terms most often confused differ in what they count and who owns them: one dealer message is a contact, opens a conversation and may create a lead, each counted by its own rule, and a listing's publication state and its enforcement overlay are held by different owners.

Each term has one plain definition and one owning chapter whose worked example settles its meaning, so a disagreement between a chapter and this page is a defect to correct in one of them, not a second meaning.

The page is built to be looked up beside a term's neighbors: sections follow the book's parts, each part's terms sit in one table with their confusable neighbors in one row or adjacent rows, every row links to its owning chapter, fictional Veldmark names stand apart in their own section, and an alphabetical index reaches every term, abbreviation and alias.

role.contribution: Gives the book one vocabulary with an owning chapter per term, so the templates and chapters can be read and checked against the same definitions.

additional_patterns.applies_to: The part sections, which follow the book's part order and with it the listing's path: business, listing model, supply, discovery, trust, money, platform, leadership.

flow.rationale: A short section on how to use the page comes first, so a reader knows the layout before the first table. The page is a lookup, so its sections group terms by the part that owns them and follow the book's order: a reader who knows which part a term belongs to finds its section without the index. The reading vocabulary (evidence labels, failure patterns) comes first because every chapter, and many rows below, use it; the Veldmark names come last so the fictional terms stay apart from the real ones; the alphabetical index closes the page because it points back into all the sections above. The parts keep the book's order because later definitions lean on earlier ones: a read model is defined from the listing system of record and a delta feed from the listing, both terms of earlier parts; with Platform before Listing, a reader looking up a read model would meet its terms before their own rows. Ordered alphabetically instead, the confusable terms of one part (contact, conversation, lead) would be split across the page and their contrast lost; with Veldmark mixed in, fictional figures would sit among real definitions.
